Chapter 7: The Limits of Reason and the Power of Experience.
You know, there’s this real temptation—especially if you’ve spent years wrestling with life’s big questions—to believe that pure reason can solve the riddle of existence. Maybe you’ve been that student, filling notebook after notebook with arguments and counterarguments. Or maybe you’re the thinker, carefully building systems to explain every detail of the world, hoping that if you just use enough logic, you’ll finally tame the absurd.
But life—well, it has this sneaky way of slipping through even the best arguments. Think about it: a sudden loss, a burst of laughter, a breathtaking moment of beauty. These aren’t things you can measure or file away neatly. They remind us that experience is always bigger than theory, and that the world is way more mysterious than any system could ever capture.
Most of us don’t even realize how much we lean on reason to keep the world at arm’s length. It’s comforting, isn’t it? To believe everything can be understood, that every question has an answer. But the absurd—it just doesn’t play by those rules. It’s that nagging sense that, no matter how hard you try, some things will always stay just out of reach.
And you know what? That’s not a sign of failure, or a lack of intelligence. It’s simply the way the world works. The absurd isn’t something you fix or solve—it’s something you live with. In fact, the more you try to explain it away, the more it seems to dance out of your grasp.
There’s actually a kind of wisdom in letting go of the need to be certain all the time. That doesn’t mean giving up on understanding. It just means recognizing that some things can only be felt, not explained. Like the taste of your favorite meal, the sound of someone you love calling your name, or the warmth of sunlight on your skin. These moments matter—even if words and theories fall short.
For a lot of people, realizing this is both humbling and freeing. It’s like discovering that life isn’t some puzzle you have to solve, but a mystery you get to live. The search for meaning doesn’t stop—it just shifts. It becomes less about finding the perfect answer, and more about truly being present, paying attention, and embracing everything that experience has to offer.
As the day winds down and the world grows quiet, the limits of reason become clearer. But so does the quiet power of experience—the simple, everyday moments that make life worth living, even when nothing seems to make sense.
